strengths: The empirical diagnosis of the failure mode is thorough and convincing: the paper documents that correct-response likelihood decays before reward drops (Fig. 2, 7), connects likelihood decay to entropy acceleration and gradient explosion (Fig. 4), and provides a well-designed controlled per-sample experiment (Fig. 3) that isolates the negative-gradient effect of GRPO on correct responses.

The observation that tool-integrated GRPO is uniquely vulnerable because correct actions are embedded within incorrect responses (Sec. 5.3, Fig. 5) and the paired case studies (Figs. 12-15) make the abstract mechanism concrete and interpretable.

The proposed LLDS regularizer is simple, lightweight, and well-motivated: the two-level selectivity (response-level gating + token-level penalty) directly follows from the analysis, and ablations on gating (Sec. 6.2), answer masking (Sec. B.3, Fig. 9), and regularization strength (Fig. 8) support the design choices.

Evaluation spans four model variants (3B/7B, Base/Instruct) and seven QA benchmarks, with training-reward curves (Fig. 6) showing consistent stabilization, and the practical-guidelines section (Sec. 7) offers actionable advice for practitioners.

The paper extends a known phenomenon (LLD from Deng et al. 2025) to a new and practically important regime (multi-turn tool-integrated RL), which constitutes useful new understanding even if the theory is largely inherited.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is limited: Theorem A.1 is explicitly a restatement of Theorem 4.4 from Deng et al. (2025), and the 'proof' mainly reduces to invoking that prior result after noting the feedback-masked GRPO objective has the same functional form. Novelty of the analysis is therefore modest, yet the abstract and intro frame LLD as newly identified ('we firstly identify').

Baseline comparisons are not fully fair: GRPO baseline numbers are taken from Jin et al. (2025) ('best checkpoint before collapse') rather than run under identical conditions, while the paper's own runs use reduced max-turn limits (2-3 vs 4 in Search-R1) — the reported +37.8%/+32.0% gains conflate the regularizer's effect with these setup differences.

The headline gains rely on the LLDS-MA variant, which is applied selectively post hoc ('we apply MA specifically to model variants where vanilla GRPO and LLDS degenerate'), introducing variant-selection bias; meanwhile results where the method underperforms (e.g., Qwen2.5-3B-Ins NQ-only +LLDS at 0.319 vs GRPO baseline 0.336 in Tab. 1) are reported without relative-change annotations, suggesting selective emphasis.

Missing comparisons with standard and relevant stabilization baselines: no KL-to-reference penalty, entropy regularization, likelihood clipping, or recent anti-collapse methods for GRPO (e.g., SimpleTIR's filtering of low-probability tokens, Dr.GRPO/DAPO-style fixes). Without these, it is unclear whether LLDS is better than simpler, already-standard remedies for the same symptom.

The causal claim that LLD is 'the core mechanism' of collapse is only correlatorily supported: the paper shows likelihood decay co-occurs with and precedes collapse, but does not provide an intervention isolating LLD from other candidate causes (e.g., off-policy ratio explosion, entropy collapse) or test LLDS on PPO to check whether the same regularizer also helps the more stable algorithm.

Reproducibility gaps: no code release is mentioned, single runs without seeds or variance estimates, and the epsilon in Definition 4.1 is left vague ('a small or non-positive constant'), making the LLD criterion under-specified.

Presentation defects: Section 5's title duplicates Section 4's ('Lazy Likelihood Displacement in Tool-Integrated GRPO'), 'PRILIMINARY' typo, Eq. (5)'s indicator/normalization notation is inconsistent, and several figures (e.g., Fig. 3 axis labels) are hard to read.

strengths: Addresses an important and practically relevant problem: training collapse in GRPO-based tool-integrated RL (Search-R1-style pipelines), which is a known pain point in the community.

Provides a reasonably detailed empirical characterization of the failure process (three-phase likelihood decay, entropy acceleration, per-sample LLD measurements in Fig. 3, ablation on regularization strength in Fig. 8), going beyond merely reporting final benchmark numbers.
Evaluates across four model configurations (Qwen2.5-3B/7B, Base/Instruct) and seven QA benchmarks, with stability curves showing that the proposed regularizer prevents collapse in all four settings.

The proposed mechanism (response-level gating plus token-level selectivity in the regularizer) is simple, cheap, and could be adopted by practitioners; the ablations on gating, answer masking, and λ give some insight into design choices.
weaknesses: Limited originality of the core contribution: Lazy Likelihood Displacement is taken from Deng et al. (2025), and Theorem 4.2 explicitly 'restates Theorem 4.4 from Deng et al. (2025)'—the proof simply invokes the prior GWHES theorem after a reduction step. The remaining novelty is applying an existing regularizer idea to the tool-integrated setting and adding gating/answer-masking heuristics.

The central causal claim—that LLD is 'the core mechanism' driving collapse—is supported only by correlational evidence (likelihood decays, entropy and gradients rise before collapse). Alternative explanations (entropy explosion, reward-hacking-style length/format failures, KL drift) are not ruled out, and the 'death spiral' (Definition 5.1) is never validated as causal, e.g., by interventions that break one link of the purported loop.

Missing the most obvious baseline: a standard KL penalty to the reference policy is precisely a likelihood-preservation regularizer, and no comparison against it (or against other stabilization methods such as entropy regularization, DAPO-style token filtering, or SimpleTIR's mitigation) is provided. Without this, it is impossible to know whether the fine-grained gating structure matters or any likelihood anchor would work.

Unfair/inconsistent baseline protocol: the GRPO baseline numbers are imported from Search-R1 (Jin et al., 2025, marked ♢) even though the authors change key training configuration (maximum turns reduced from 4 to 2 or 3, which they state improves efficiency and could plausibly change stability). Comparing their method trained under one configuration against a baseline's reported number from a different configuration undermines the headline gains (+37.8%, +32.0%).

Results are inconsistent with a stable story: e.g., Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct NQ-only +LLDS drops well below baseline on 2Wiki (0.298 vs. 0.386) and Musique while the abstract claims consistent gains; the choice between LLDS and LLDS-MA appears post hoc per configuration ('we switch to LLDS-MA when stronger encouragement of tool usage is desired'), raising concern about variant selection on test performance. No variance, seeds, or significance testing is reported for any comparison.

Presentation issues: Section 3 is titled 'PRILIMINARY' (misspelled); Sections 4 and 5 share nearly the same title; 'LLD' names both the phenomenon and a regularizer variant, making Eq. (4) vs. (5) confusing; Definition 4.1 states J(θfin) < J(θold), which contradicts objective maximization; plus several typos ('accerlerrated', 'unstable'/'unst able', 'resolved the collapse issue'). These suggest the manuscript was not carefully polished.

No statement of limitations, no discussion of compute/seeds/hyperparameter sensitivity beyond λ, and no code or artifact release mentioned, which weakens reproducibility for a paper whose contribution is largely an empirical training recipe.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and practically important problem: training collapse in GRPO-based tool-integrated RL (Search-R1-style pipelines), which is widely observed but poorly explained.

The empirical characterization of the failure trajectory (early stagnation, steady likelihood decay, accelerated collapse with entropy spikes and gradient inflation) is detailed and includes useful controlled evidence, e.g., per-sample single-update LLD measurements (Fig. 3), entropy/length controls (Fig. 4), and analysis of correct actions embedded in incorrect responses (Fig. 5).

The proposed LLDS regularizer is simple, lightweight, and well-motivated by the analysis: response-level gating plus token-level selectivity targets only likelihood-reducing tokens in globally-declining responses, minimizing interference with GRPO's normal updates.

Evaluation breadth is substantial: four model configurations (Qwen2.5-3B/7B, Base/Instruct), two training configurations, and seven QA benchmarks, plus reward-curve evidence across all four settings showing baseline GRPO collapse and LLDS stability (Fig. 6).

Ablations on regularization strength (Fig. 8) and on the answer-masking variant (Fig. 9, Sec. B.3) provide some insight into design choices, and case studies in Appendix C concretize the mechanisms (prefix-similarity and low-likelihood long trajectories).
weaknesses: Limited originality of the core analysis: LLD is taken from Deng et al. (2025), and the paper's Theorem 4.2/A.1 is explicitly a restatement of Deng et al.'s Theorem 4.4 applied to tool-integrated settings, with the proof consisting of directly invoking that prior result. The theoretical contribution is largely adaptation rather than new understanding.

Causality of the 'LLD Death Spiral' is asserted but only supported by correlational training-dynamics plots. No intervention isolates LLD as the causal driver (e.g., artificially freezing likelihoods, or perturbing one link in the claimed spiral) — the strongest claims ('fundamental bottleneck', 'self-reinforcing spiral') exceed the evidence.

Baseline fairness concerns: the GRPO baseline is quoted from Search-R1 (best checkpoint before collapse) rather than retrained under identical conditions, and the authors reduce max turns from 4 to 2–3 for their runs. Comparing their method trained under one configuration against baseline numbers from a different configuration weakens the headline gains; several rows in Tables 1–2 mix results reproduced under different settings with numbers imported from Jin et al. (2025).

Headline improvements (+37.8%, +32.0%) are relative gains over a collapsed/degenerate baseline; absolute EM improvements are more modest (e.g., 0.312→0.430). Also, LLDS-MA is applied selectively per model/setting (only where LLDS 'degenerates into a single search call'), which risks inflating the reported averages relative to a uniform protocol.

No comparison against other standard stabilization baselines (e.g., KL regularization strength sweeps, entropy bonuses, lower learning rates, gradient clipping, DAPO-style modifications, or SimpleTIR's mitigation), so it is unclear whether fine-grained likelihood regularization is necessary or whether simpler fixes suffice.
Single-run results with no variance estimates across seeds, and no release/code statement in the manuscript, limiting reproducibility confidence.
No limitations section or ethical-considerations discussion.

Presentation is rough: duplicated section titles (Sections 4 and 5 are identically titled 'Lazy Likelihood Displacement in Tool-Integrated GRPO'), typos ('PRILIMINARY', 'accerlerrated', 'watch for correct actions...' as a heading), grammatical issues ('selectively regularize ... and resolved the collapse issue'), and a somewhat cluttered experimental setup where the best-performing method varies per row (LLD, LLDS, LLDS-MA), making the main recommendation harder to follow.

strengths: The paper identifies and carefully characterizes a practically important failure mode ('Lazy Likelihood Displacement') in GRPO-based tool-integrated RL, with a clear three-phase empirical trajectory (stagnation, steady decay, acceleration) documented across multiple model scales and variants (Qwen2.5-3B/7B, Base/Instruct, plus Llama3.2 in the appendix).

The diagnostic analysis is unusually thorough for this area: controlled single-update per-sample LLD measurements, entropy/response-length/valid-search dynamics, token-likelihood before vs. after tool feedback as a function of interaction rounds, and concrete paired case studies (Figures 12-15) that make the embedding-similarity and low-likelihood mechanisms tangible.

The proposed LLDS regularizer is simple, well-motivated (action-level gating + token-level selectivity), and ablated seriously: token vs. response vs. action gating variants, regularization strength lambda, and an answer-masking variant for models that degenerate to single-turn search.

Results are broad: seven QA benchmarks, integration with GSPO demonstrating the fix is not GRPO-specific, favorable comparisons against dense-reward methods (StepSearch, CriticSearch, TreeGRPO) using only outcome rewards, and full training curves showing collapse prevention rather than only endpoint metrics.
Honest accounting of the GRPO baseline (best checkpoint before collapse) and disclosure of setup deviations (max turns 4->3) support reproducibility; code and models are released.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is largely an adaptation of Deng et al. (2025)'s GWHS analysis from single-turn GRPO to the multi-turn/tool-integrated setting; the proof reduces to re-applying their theorem conditionally per action and summing. This limits originality of the formal component, and the 'informal' theorem statements plus heuristic conditions in Definition A.3 weaken the theoretical rigor.

Causality is asserted but only partially established: the evidence shows likelihood decay precedes and correlates with collapse (and the controlled single-update study is a good start), but a direct intervention study showing that suppressing LLD specifically - rather than adding any likelihood/entropy-stabilizing term - causes the improvement would strengthen the claim that LLD is 'the' core mechanism. A comparison to simpler stabilizers (e.g., plain KL-to-init increase, entropy bonuses, or likelihood-floor clipping without gating) is missing.

Evaluation rigor gaps: all RL runs appear to be single-seed with no variance or significance reporting, which is a real concern given that GRPO collapse timing is known to be stochastic; several baseline numbers are imported from other papers (dagger/diamond notation) under potentially different retrieval corpora, turn budgets, and training configurations, making the dense-reward comparisons indicative rather than strictly controlled.

Reported GRPO baselines are noticeably lower than some published Search-R1 numbers (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B GRPO at 0.350 here vs. ~0.40+ elsewhere), raising questions about baseline strength; while the 'best checkpoint before collapse' convention favors GRPO, the reduced max-turn budget and fixed setup could still understate the baseline, inflating relative gains.

Generalization of the central claim ('structural failure mode of GRPO-based TIR') is demonstrated only on search-based QA; other tool types (code execution, SQL) are cited as motivation but not tested, so the reach of the diagnosis and the fix remains specialized.

Presentation issues: the abstract's headline numbers (+45.2%, +37.1%) refer to Base models while Instruct gains are smaller, which could mislead; some figures (e.g., Figure 3b, Figure 5) are difficult to parse without careful reading; informal/formal theorem pairs are loosely connected.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant problem: catastrophic training collapse in GRPO-based tool-integrated RL (Search-R1 style pipelines), which is consistently observed across systems.

The empirical characterization of the failure is fairly thorough: three-phase likelihood dynamics, entropy explosion, per-sample likelihood degradation, effect of OOD tool feedback and number of tool-interaction rounds (Figures 2–6), supported by case studies in the appendix.

The proposed LLDS regularizer is lightweight, requires no extra models or ground-truth step supervision, and is evaluated extensively: four Qwen model variants (3B/7B, Base/Instruct), Llama3.2-3B, GSPO integration, ablations over λ, gating granularity (token/response/action-level), and comparison against dense-reward baselines (StepSearch, CriticSearch, TreeGRPO).

Reproducibility appears reasonable: hyperparameters, corpus, retriever, and training setup are described in detail, code and models are linked, and the baseline protocol (best checkpoint before collapse) is stated to be generous to GRPO.
The paper is transparent that LLD builds on Deng et al. (2025) and clearly delineates its multi-turn extension rather than claiming the base phenomenon as new.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. The central theoretical contribution (Theorem A.1) is obtained essentially by applying the existing GWHS theorem of Deng et al. (2025) conditionally on the prefix including tool feedback and summing over turns (the proof itself concedes this reduction: 'has exactly the same functional form as the standard GRPO objective'). The 'tool-integrated' aspect enters mainly through the conditioning context, not through a fundamentally new analysis of multi-turn dynamics.

The two purported structural causes of LLD in TI-GRPO — low likelihood of incorrect responses and embedding similarity between correct/incorrect trajectories — are asserted more than established. The 'observation match ratio' heuristic (Figure 5) is a proxy for 'correct actions inside incorrect responses', and embedding similarity is only supported by two anecdotal case studies rather than systematic measurement. Alternative explanations (training–inference mismatch, off-policy drift; Liu et al., 2025; Xue et al., 2025) are discussed but not experimentally ruled out.

The method is a fairly direct application of known ideas (likelihood-preservation penalties related to Razin et al. 2024's likelihood displacement in DPO, and standard KL/trust-region style regularization), packaged with heuristic gating and answer-token reweighting (LLDS-MA). The MA variant with a schedule β = min(V_s/V_B, 1) feels ad hoc, tuned per model (λ = 0.2 except 0.3 for one model), and its justification is post-hoc.

A substantial portion of the headline gains (+37–45%) comes from the baseline collapsing rather than from a comparison of converged performance. While the best-checkpoint protocol is reasonable, the paper does not disentangle how much of the improvement is 'prevents collapse' versus 'improves optimization', and does not test simpler collapse mitigations (e.g., stronger KL penalty, lower learning rate, earlier stopping, entropy regularization) as baselines. Figure 8 shows λ = 0.01 delays collapse — suggesting a simple KL-style knob may already capture much of the effect.

Evaluation is confined to a single task family (search-based QA with EM) and a fixed retriever/corpus. Generalization of both the LLD diagnosis and LLDS to other tool types (code execution, multimodal), other reward structures, or larger scales is only asserted as future work, weakening the claim that LLD is 'the' structural failure mode of TI-RL.

The formal 'LLD Death Spiral' definition (Definition A.3) uses existential constants (ε, δ, c) whose conditions (e.g., monotone expected decay, self-amplifying magnitude) are never verified quantitatively in the experiments; it functions as narrative framing rather than a falsifiable characterization.

Presentation issues: key definitions appear twice in informal and formal versions with inconsistencies (e.g., ε ≤ 0 vs. ε < 0 across Definition 5.1 and A.3), Figure 1 reports relative percentages without absolute deltas in text, and several mechanism claims in Section 5.4 rely on figures with hard-to-parse dual axes.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper identifies a concrete failure mode (LLD) in tool-integrated GRPO and characterizes it empirically with a three-phase trajectory (stagnation, steady decay, acceleration), supported by compelling visualizations (Figures 2-6) that link likelihood decay, entropy explosion, and gradient magnitude.

The theoretical contribution, while adapted, is a reasonable extension of the GWHS analysis (Deng et al., 2025) to the multi-turn, feedback-masked tool-integrated setting, and the two structural factors (low-likelihood incorrect responses, embedding similarity) are backed by targeted experiments (Figures 5, 6, 9, and case studies in Appendix C).

Comprehensive evaluation: two model families (Qwen2.5-3B/7B, Base/Instruct), an additional Llama3.2-3B result, integration with GSPO, ablations over regularization strength and gating variants (token/response/action-level), and comparisons against dense-reward baselines (StepSearch, CriticSearch, Tree-GRPO) - all while using only outcome rewards. Strong relative gains (+45.2%, +37.1%, +22.0%) and consistent training-stability results across all four Qwen variants (Figure 7).
Good reproducibility: code and models are released, and hyperparameters, corpus/retriever setup, and baseline descriptions are documented in detail (Appendix B).
The LLDS-MA variant is an interesting practical finding - relaxing regularization on answer tokens unlocks emergent multi-turn search behavior (Figure 9b), which adds value beyond pure stabilization.
weaknesses: The theory is largely a reduction of the existing GWHS theorem to conditional distributions ('Reduction to standard GRPO at the action level'); the extension is more of an adaptation than a new result, and the connection between the theory (negative-gradient interference from incorrect responses) and the proposed fix (penalizing likelihood decreases of preserved responses) is loose rather than derived.

Causality is not fully established: the claim that LLD is 'the primary cause' of collapse rests partly on correlational evidence (LLD precedes reward collapse) plus the fact that LLDS prevents collapse. Alternative explanations (e.g., training-inference mismatch) are discussed but not experimentally ruled out.

Reported gains partially reflect stabilization of a collapsing baseline rather than superior learning; while using the best pre-collapse checkpoint for GRPO is fair, no seed variance, confidence intervals, or repeated runs are reported for the benchmark tables, which is a notable omission given the volatility of the phenomenon being studied.

Scope is narrow: a single task domain (search-integrated QA with a fixed E5 retriever), one set of small models, and a heuristic method (hinge penalty with action-level gating plus hand-tuned schedules like beta = min(V_s/V_B, 1)) raise questions about generality to other tools (code execution, APIs) that the paper only gestures toward in future work.

The method introduces several design choices justified mainly by ablation rather than principle (action-level vs. response-level gating, MA applied only to model variants that degenerate to single-turn search, lambda = 0.2 default with 0.3 for one model), which weakens the sense that the regularizer is a principled solution to the identified mechanism.
